newsitem.title: MEXICO: Latam stocks hoping to recover from Dow spill.
newsitem.headline: Latam stocks hoping to recover from Dow spill.

text.p: Rocked by last week's Dow tumble, Latin American markets could continue their slide this week, but Latin American stock-watchers said they held out some hopes for a rebound.

Analysts see Wall Street as a continuing key factor in Latin American stock behavior as last week's shakiness in the Dow, sparked by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's warnings of inflationary risks and excessive market optimism, led to parallel slides south of the U.S. border.
"The market will continue to be tremendously sensitive to movements in the Dow," said Guillermo Tagle, head of research at Santander Investment in Santiago, Chile.
Markets could remain stable, however, as some analysts said a hike in U.S. interest rates has already been discounted.
"I think they've already discounted a hike in interest rates, but they will keep a very close eye on the peso," said Rodolfo Campuzano, an equity analyst at Mexico City's Invex brokerage.

Mexico's blue chip IPC index ended last week down 1.03 percent at 3,840.98 points even though it posted a record close of 3,938.69 on Tuesday following short-lived macro-economic optimism. Jitters over the U.S. certification of Mexico's cooperation in drug-combatting efforts contributed to the market's volatility, analysts said. They added the U.S. Congress challenge to President Bill Clinton could put further pressure on stocks.
In Brazil, U.S. interest rate uncertainty was seen adding to market fears over an ongoing congressional probe into irregularities in the dealing of state and municipal bonds.

A worst-case scenario could be a broad congressional inquiry into Brazil's financial sector, analysts said, which would end up distracting lawmakers from the much-awaited approval of key constitutional reforms. Brazil shares .BVSP rose 1.2 percent last week to close at points 8,829 on Friday.
Argentina dealers said they expected the market to bounce back this week after a streak of profit-taking, which dealers blamed on Wall Street's tumble following Greenspan's comments.
The blue-chip MerVal index shed 3.1 percent last week to 713.59, trimming February gains to 3.6 percent.
"We are now strictly conditioned by movements on Wall Street -- local economic fundamentals remain very good and cash flows are strong," said Jorge Bonanno at Interfin brokers.

A final surge of corporate fourth-quarter reports could also steer markets, analysts said. Results to date have been mixed. Chilean markets could see some price corrections as investors look for overpriced stocks based on earnings reports, which must be released there by Monday.
The selective .IPSA index ended last week down 0.08 percent at 115.97 points.
In Caracas stocks investors were seen watching for the dust to clear on budgetary and inflationary implications of a recent public sector wage deal.

February's inflation fell to 2.3 percent from 2.6 percent in January, the Central Bank said Friday. But after the Venezuelan government granted workers a 50 percent-plus public sector pay increase last week, many fear inflation will end the year double current official targets of 25 to 35 percent.
The bolsa's 19-share .IBC index closed the week broadly flat, off 0.1 pct at 6709.43.
